column4: ### The Body
column5: ### The Body

column4: The church is often described as **the Body of Christ**, emphasizing both its unity and diversity. With Christ as the head, the church functions as a living organism where every believer plays an essential and potentially diverse role. Each member is uniquely gifted and contributes to the health and mission of the body according to their own function. This image highlights the interdependence of believers, specifically that the body must be connected to function, and that our function is collaborative not competitive. When every part works together, the body grows and thrives in unity and love (1 Corinthians 12:12-27; Ephesians 4:15-16; Colossians 1:18).
column5: The church is often described as the **Body of Christ**, which emphasizes both its unity and its diversity. With Christ as the head, the church functions as a living body in which each believer plays an essential role that may differ. Each member is uniquely gifted and contributes to the health and work of the body according to his or her function. This image highlights the interdependence of believers, namely that the body must be joined together to function, and that our work is cooperative rather than competitive. When each part works together, the body grows and thrives in unity and love (1 Corinthians 12:12-27; Ephesians 4:15-16; Colossians 1:18).

column4: ### The Bride
column5: ### The Bride

column4: The church is described as **the Bride of Christ**, this reflects an intimate and loving relationship with Jesus. Just as a bride is cherished and made ready for her husband, the church is sanctified and purified by Christ’s sacrificial love. This metaphor captures the devotion and faithfulness expected of the church, as well as the deep affection Christ has for His people. The imagery also points to the ultimate union between Christ and the church, celebrated in the marriage supper of the Lamb, where the church is presented in glory without spot or blemish (Ephesians 5:25-27; Revelation 19:7-9; Revelation 21:2).
column5: The church is described as the **Bride of Christ**, which reflects the close, loving relationship it has with Jesus. Like a bride who is honored and prepared for her husband, the church is sanctified and cleansed by the self-sacrificial love of Christ. This metaphor captures the devotion and faithfulness expected of the church, as well as the deep love Christ has for his people. This image also points to the final union between Christ and the church, celebrated at the marriage supper of the Lamb, where the church is presented in glory, without spot or blemish (Ephesians 5:25-27; Revelation 19:7-9; Revelation 21:2).

column4: ### The Temple
column5: ### The Temple

column4: The church is described as **the Temple of God**, the dwelling place of His Spirit. Believers are described as living stones being built together on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Himself as the cornerstone. This holy structure signifies God’s presence among His people and their role as a community of worship and prayer. The temple imagery underscores the importance of holiness and the church’s collective purpose in glorifying God (1 Corinthians 3:16-17; Ephesians 2:19-22; 1 Peter 2:4-5).
column5: The church is described as the **Temple of God**, the dwelling place of His Spirit. Believers are depicted as living stones being built together upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ himself as the cornerstone. This holy structure symbolizes God’s presence among his people and their role as a community of worship and prayer. The temple imagery underscores the importance of holiness and the shared purpose of the church in glorifying God (1 Corinthians 3:16-17; Ephesians 2:19-22; 1 Peter 2:4-5).

column4: ### The Family
column5: ### The Family

column4: The church is described as **the Family of God**, emphasizing relational unity and care among its members. Through the Spirit of adoption, believers are made children of God and members of His household. This familial imagery highlights the love, belonging, and shared inheritance believers have in Christ. It also reflects the call to treat one another with compassion and humility as brothers and sisters in God’s family (Galatians 6:10; Ephesians 2:19; Romans 8:15-17). Furthermore, through the family image it depicts how the members of the church are to become mature, that they would be taught and nourished by spiritual mothers and fathers (1 Timothy 5:1-2), that we could go from infants drinking the pure milk of the Word, to full grown adults able to eat the strong meat of the Word (Hebrews 5).
column5: The church is described as the **Family of God**, which emphasizes the relational unity and care among its members. Through the Spirit of adoption, believers are made children of God and members of his household. This family imagery expresses the love, belonging, and shared inheritance that believers have in Christ. It also reflects the call to treat one another with compassion and humility as siblings in the family of God (Galatians 6:10; Ephesians 2:19; Romans 8:15-17). Furthermore, through the family imagery it shows how members of the church become mature, being taught and nourished by spiritual mothers and fathers (1 Timothy 5:1-2), so that we move from infants drinking the pure milk of the Word to mature adults able to eat the solid meat of the Word (Hebrews 5).

column4: ### The Flock
column5: ### The Flock

column4: The church is described as **the Flock**, sheep under the care of Jesus, the Good Shepherd. This image conveys the church’s dependence on Christ for guidance, sustenance, and protection. It also emphasizes the responsibility of church leaders to faithfully shepherd God’s flock as under shepherds, mirroring Christ’s example of love and care. The flock imagery speaks to trust, obedience, and the close relationship between the Great Shepherd and His sheep (John 10:14-16; 1 Peter 5:2; Acts 20:28).
column5: The church is depicted as the **Flock**, the sheep under the care of Jesus, the Good Shepherd. This image conveys the church’s dependence on Christ for guidance, nourishment, and protection. It also underscores the responsibility of church leaders to shepherd the flock of God faithfully as under-shepherds, imitating Christ’s example of love and care. The flock imagery speaks of trust, obedience, and the close relationship between the Great Shepherd and his sheep (John 10:14-16; 1 Peter 5:2; Acts 20:28).

column4: ### The Vine and Branches
column5: ### The Vine and Its Branches

column4: The church is described as **the Vine and Branches**, illustrating the essential connection between believers and Christ. Jesus is the true vine, and believers are the branches that must remain in Him to bear fruit. This metaphor highlights dependence on Christ for spiritual vitality, growth, and productivity. Without Him, believers can do nothing, but by abiding in Him, they glorify God and fulfill their purpose. Jesus will prune so that He can bear more fruit in our lives (John 15:1-5).
column5: The church is described as the **Vine and its Branches**, which depicts the indispensable relationship between believers and Christ. Jesus is the true vine, and believers are the branches who must remain in him in order to bear fruit. This metaphor shows dependence on Christ for spiritual vitality, growth, and fruitfulness. Apart from him, believers can do nothing, but by abiding in him they glorify God and fulfill their purpose. Jesus will prune in order to produce more fruit in our lives (John 15:1-5).

column4: ## Roles of the Church
column5: ## The Role of the Church

column4: The church’s mission, like the Holy Spirit's role, can be understood through three dimensions: upward, inward, and outward, each reflecting a unique aspect of its calling in God’s plan. These dimensions guide the church in fulfilling its role as a worshiping, edifying, and missional community.

These directions guide the church as it fulfills its role as a worshiping, edifying, and missional community.

column4: ### Upward: Worship and Glorifying God
column5: ### Upward: Worship and Praise of God

column4: The church’s first purpose is to worship and glorify God. Corporate worship, where believers gather to exalt God together, is a visible reflection of His glory and a response to His greatness. As the psalmist declares, “*Worship the Lord in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth*” (Psalms 96:9). Beyond corporate worship, the church is called to live lives of obedience and sacrifice, offering themselves as “living sacrifices” as an act of spiritual worship (Romans 12:1-2). This upward focus keeps the church centered on God’s majesty and aligns its priorities with His will.
column5: The primary purpose of the church is to worship and praise God. Corporate worship, where believers gather to magnify God together, is a visible reflection of His glory and a response to His greatness. As the psalmist says, “*Worship the Lord in the beauty of holiness; tremble before Him, all the earth*” (Psalms 96:9). Beyond corporate worship, the church is called to live in obedience and sacrifice, offering themselves as “living sacrifices” as an act of spiritual worship (Romans 12:1-2). This upward focus keeps the church centered on the honor of God and aligns it with prioritizing His will.

column4: The church at Jerusalem was led primarily by the **apostles**, who focused on teaching, prayer, and spiritual oversight (Acts 2:42, Acts 6:4). As the community grew, the need for administrative structure became apparent, particularly to address practical matters like caring for widows and distributing resources. This led to the appointment of **deacons** (Acts 6:1-7). These individuals, chosen for their spiritual maturity and good reputation, handled practical ministries to allow the apostles to focus on their spiritual responsibilities. Over time, **elders** also emerged as leaders in the Jerusalem church. For instance, during the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15), both apostles and elders were involved in decision-making, showing a collaborative leadership structure.
column5: The church in Jerusalem was led primarily by the **apostles**, who focused on teaching, prayer, and spiritual oversight (Acts 2:42, Acts 6:4). As the community grew, the need for administrative structure became evident, especially to address practical matters such as caring for widows and distributing resources. This led to the appointment of **deacons** (Acts 6:1-7). These individuals, chosen for their spiritual maturity and good reputation, managed practical ministries so that the apostles could devote themselves to their spiritual responsibilities. Over time, **elders** also emerged as leaders in the Jerusalem church. For example, during the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15), both the apostles and the elders participated in decision-making, demonstrating a shared leadership model.

column4: ### Church at Antioch
column5: ### The Church in Antioch

column4: The church at Antioch had a more decentralized and diverse leadership structure compared to Jerusalem. It was led by a group of **prophets and teachers**, including Barnabas, Saul (Paul), Simeon, Lucius, and Manaen (Acts 13:1). The church at Antioch was also much more oriented towards reaching the gentiles, where the church in Jerusalem reflected more of its Jewish roots. While the New Testament does not explicitly mention deacons in Antioch, it is likely that practical roles existed given the church's growing size and involvement in sending relief to Jerusalem (Acts 11:29-30). The church at Antioch became a model for commissioning missionaries, with leaders praying, fasting, and laying hands on Paul and Barnabas to send them out (Acts 13:2-3). This demonstrates a structure that balanced spiritual oversight (prophets and teachers) with missional outreach and practical support.

It was led by a group of **prophets and teachers**, including Barnabas, Saul (Paul), Simeon, Lucius, and Manaen (Acts 13:1). The Antioch church was also heavily engaged in outreach to the Gentiles, while the Jerusalem church reflected its Jewish roots. Although the New Testament does not explicitly mention deacons in Antioch, it is likely that practical ministries existed as the church grew and was involved in sending relief to Jerusalem (Acts 11:29-30). The Antioch church became a model for sending missionaries, with its leaders praying, fasting, and laying hands on Paul and Barnabas to commission them (Acts 13:2-3). This demonstrates a structure that balances spiritual oversight (prophets and teachers) with evangelistic outreach and practical support.

column4: Unlike Paul’s corrections to the Corinthians and Galatians, the scriptures do not critique the leadership structures of Jerusalem or Antioch. This suggests that these churches, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, were free to adapt their gatherings to meet their unique needs and circumstances within the framework of sound doctrine and apostolic teaching (Acts 2:42, 2 Timothy 3:16-17).

column4: ## Leadership Versus Gifting
column5: ## Leadership and Giftedness

column4: A commonly misunderstood aspect of leadership in the church is the separation between the authority and responsibility of leadership, and specific giftings.
column5: A commonly misunderstood point about church leadership is distinguishing between the authority and responsibility of leadership and particular gifts.

column4: This confusion is centered on our use of words like teacher, paster, prophet, apostle, evangelist. These words are gifts. There is not an **office** of ‘apostle’ in the New Testament church. There are people who do the work of an apostle, who have the gift or calling of apostle. Having the gift of apostle does not give them authority of responsibility.
column5: This mistake is rooted in how we use words like teacher, pastor, prophet, apostle, evangelist. These terms are gifts. There is no **office** of ‘apostle’ in the New Testament church. There are people who do the work of an apostle, who have the gift or calling of an apostle. Possessing an apostolic gift does not confer authority or responsibility.

column4: Likewise, there are people gifted in being a pastor/shepherd, but that does not make them ‘THE PASTOR’ of the local church or make them ‘your’ pastor. The five-fold ministry gifts do not lead the church, the leaders (elders and deacons) do. It is very common for leaders to have specific five-fold ministry gifts, but that gift enhances their leadership, it doesn’t create it. Likewise, it's common for still-developing people with fivefold giftings to serve and aspire to leadership, but God is first interested in character, then interested in giftings. We are all to become mature, able to discern the word of God, full of the spirit, and doing good works.

column4: ## Your Role in the Church
column5: ## Your Role in the Church

column4: So far in this chapter we’ve covered the leadership of the church and the core analogies for the church. Let’s build upon the specific analogy of *the body* and consider a marathon runner.
column5: Up to this point in the chapter we have discussed church leadership and the central, foundational examples for the church. Let us build on the specific example of the *body* and consider a marathon runner.

column4: ### You Are a Part of the Whole
column5: ### You Are Part of the Whole

column4: The church, as the Body of Christ, depends on every member working together to fulfill its mission. Just as the body cannot function properly if one part is missing, the church needs each believer to actively participate, grow, and serve. Each member of the body has a very important role. To be part of the body means staying connected. A body can survive at diminished capacity without a limb, but the limb itself cannot live when separated from the body. We must be an active part of the church and not become dismembered. Hebrews 10:24 says that we should gather and not forsake the assembly.
column5: The church, since it is the Body of Christ, depends on every member working together to accomplish its purpose. Just as the body cannot function properly if one member is missing, so too the church needs every believer to participate actively, grow, and serve. Every member of the body has a very important role. Being part of the body means remaining connected. The body can continue to live, though weakened, without a member, but the member itself cannot live when cut off from the body. We must be an active part of the church and not be disconnected. Hebrews 10:24 says that we should come together and not neglect the assembling.

column4: To really work and function together you need to fellowship! You need to know others, love others and ideally like others! Build strong relationships and friendships and repair them when they become stressed or injured. When a joint gets injured or inflamed, you need to work to rest and or reset it; so that the joint that’s dislodged doesn’t become broken! A broken and unhealing limb will eventually be separated, and you cannot be part of the body, alone.
column5: To truly fit together and function you need brotherhood! You must know others, love others, and get the best from others! Build strong relationships and friendships, and repair them when they become strained or injured. When a joint is injured or inflamed, you must work to rest it or reset it; so that a dislocated joint does not break! A broken member that does not heal is eventually amputated, and you cannot be a part of the body by yourself.

column4: We don’t all have the same function. Some of us may share the Gospel from a stage, others around a dinner table. But we are ALL called to be ministers of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18-19). We have all been received into the priesthood of believers (1 Peter 2:9, Revelation 1:6). This means that we're all supposed to be able to do the work of the ministry by the power of the Holy Spirit.

This means that we all can do the work of ministry, empowered by the Holy Spirit.

column4: ### You Need Training
column5: ### You Need Training

column4: Believers must train and equip for their unique roles in the church, just as a runner strengthens specific muscles for the race. You won’t be successful if you jump into a marathon and haven’t trained, and not all training is equal, you need to be adequately prepared for the race. Jesus has given specific ministry gifts to equip believers, not to do all the work themselves, but to empower every member to serve effectively in their unique roles.

You will not succeed if you jump into a marathon without training, and not all training is the same; you need to prepare adequately for the race. Jesus gave specific ministry gifts to equip believers, not so that they would do all the work themselves, but to strengthen each member to serve effectively in their particular role.

column4: Training for a marathon will bring about transformation. You need strength and you need to transform. It’s our responsibility to submit ourselves to God and let him transform us in renewal (Romans 12:1-2). Transformation should lead you to maturity, enabling you to bear your own loads and support others. You should be able to bear MUCH fruit. This will be discussed at length in the chapter on sanctification.

column4: Training is hard, sometimes it’s uncomfortable. Sometimes the transformation you need to go through you’d much rather skip. column5: As individuals, we must first submit ourselves to God, and then, in this context, to a body of believers. Submission in the church means honoring divine leadership (Hebrews 13:17) and submitting to one another in mutual submission (Ephesians 5:21).

column4: Submission can be difficult, especially when you have experienced broken trust or failed leadership previously. This does not imply blind obedience or control but reflects a spirit of reverence and cooperation. Worldly submission is demanded by those in authority and can be degrading and lead to resentment. Biblical submission rooted in humility and discernment strengthens the church and fosters accountability. Be willing to listen to guidance and constructive feedback.

column4: Practice giving. We can give to the church in many important ways, and we are instructed to do so to accomplish the mission.
column5: Practice giving. We can contribute to the church in many meaningful ways, and we are commanded to do so to accomplish the mission.

column4: - Time - we can give our time and volunteer. When we give our time, we use our efforts and our talents. This can also be a great way to learn new skills and increase existing ones.
column5: - Time - we can give our time and volunteer. When we give our time, we are using our efforts and gifts. This can also be a great way to learn new skills and enhance existing ones.

column4: - Resources - we can give of our resources. Most commonly today this is probably giving financially to the church and to ministries (not just the “institution”, but those in need in the church). Giving money is useful, because the church can buy needed resources with it, but people have given their physical resources beyond money, for example extra homes, clothing, cars, food, building materials, tools, etc. In Acts 4:32-35 we see an example of early believers giving freely, sharing proceeds from sale of extra lands and homes and giving so that ‘none had need’.
column5: - Resources - we can give our resources. Today this most often means financial giving to the church and ministries (not only the “organization”, but also those in need within the church). Monetary giving is helpful, because the church can purchase needed resources, but people have also given physical resources beyond money, for example extra homes, clothing, cars, food, building materials, equipment, etc. In Acts 4:32-35 we see an example of the early believers giving freely, sharing proceeds from the sale of land and extra houses and giving so that ‘no one was in need’.

column4: Working alongside others in ministry can reveal your strengths and deepen your understanding of your role. Engage in small groups or church activities to foster connections. Listen to the burdens and needs of those around you and consider how you can support them. Building relationships within the church helps you connect with others and understand the community’s needs.
column5: Working with others within ministry can reveal your strengths and deepen your understanding of your role. Participate in small groups or church activities to build connections. Listen to the burdens and needs of those around you and consider how you can support them. Building relationships within the church helps you connect with others and understand the needs of the community.

column4: #### Step 4 - Get Help!
column5: #### Step 4 - Seek Help!

column4: Jesus said that in life we would experience trouble! (John 16:33) We are encouraged to not carry the weight of our burdens by ourselves but to cast them on God who cares for us! (1 Peter 5:7)
column5: Jesus said that in life we will face trouble! (John 16:33) We are encouraged not to carry the weight of our burdens alone but to cast them on God who cares for us! (1 Peter 5:7)

column4: Sometimes in our journey we may become injured. Marathon runners, even when doing “everything right” can stress their bodies to the point of injury, or they can trip and fall.
column5: Sometimes in our journey we can be injured. Marathon runners, even when they are doing “everything right,” can put strain on their bodies that causes injury, or they can stumble and fall.

column4: Not all ‘falling’ is sin related, but some of it is, not all weakness is ‘our fault’, sometimes others will sin against us. Regardless for the cause of our weakness or injury we are to be restored and healed.
column5: Not all ‘falls’ are related to sin, though some are; not all weakness is ‘our fault,’ and sometimes others sin against us. Regardless of the cause of our weakness or injury, we need to be restored and healed.

column4: There is great freedom in seeking inner healing and restoration. We are called to cover the vulnerable parts of the body (1 Corinthians 12:23) and to restore those caught in trespasses (Galatians 6:1).
column5: There is great freedom in seeking inner healing and restoration. We are called to cover the weaker parts of the body (1 Corinthians 12:23) and to restore those caught in transgressions (Galatians 6:1).

column4: There is much to say about this topic, and we explore the themes of healing as an overview in the chapter on sanctification.
column5: Much can be said on this topic, and we broadly explore healing themes in the chapter on sanctification.

column4: #### Step 5 - Be Patient
column5: #### Step 5 - Be Patient

column4: Pay attention to confirmation from God and others. Often, God confirms your calling through fruitfulness, joy, and affirmation from those around you. Reflect on where your efforts have borne fruit and listen to feedback about the impact of the ministry. This can help you recognize where you are most effective in serving the Body of Christ.
column5: Pay attention to affirmation that comes from God and others. Often, God confirms your calling through fruitfulness, joy, and affirmation from those around you. Reflect on where your efforts have borne fruit and listen to feedback about the impact of your ministry. This can help you recognize where you are most effective in serving the Body of Christ.

column4: Be patient and trust God’s timing. Discovering your role may take time and involve trial and error (Philippians 1:6). Trust that God will guide you as you remain faithful and open to His leading. During this time, commit to growth and training by attending workshops, Bible studies, and other resources that equip you for service. Do this with the church, engage with the body of Christ to discover your gifting.
column5: Be patient and trust God’s timing. Discovering your role can take time and may involve trial and error (Philippians 1:6). Trust that God will guide you as you remain faithful and open to His leading. During this time, commit to growth and training by attending workshops, Bible studies, and other resources that equip you for ministry. Do this alongside the church, engaging with the Body of Christ to discern your gifts.

column4: Remember, the church is not a building or an institution; it is a living, breathing body made up of people like you. By stepping into your role, you contribute to its mission and glorify Christ as its head.
column5: Remember, the church is not a building or an institution; it is a living, breathing body made up of people like you. By taking up your role, you contribute to its mission and glorify Christ, who is its head.

column4: ## Personal Reflection Questions
column5: ## Personal Reflection Questions

column4: 1.  What does it mean to you personally to be a “called-out one”? How can you live out this identity in your daily life?
column5: 1.  What does it mean to you to be “called”? How can you live out this identity in your daily life?

column4: 2.  Which of the biblical images of the church (Body, Bride, Temple, etc.) resonates most with you? Why?
column5: 2.  Which of the biblical images of the church (Body, Bride, Temple, etc.) most impacts you? Why?

column4: 3.  Reflect on your role in the Body of Christ. What gifts, talents, or passions has God given you to serve His church?
column5: 3.  Reflect on your role in the Body of Christ. What kinds of gifts, abilities, or passions has God given you to serve His church?

column4: 4.  How does being part of a local church strengthen your faith and help you fulfill God’s mission?
column5: 4.  How does belonging to a local church strengthen your faith and help you fulfill God’s mission?

column4: 5.  What steps can you take to foster unity, accountability, and growth in your church community?
column5: 5.  What steps can you take to cultivate unity, accountability, and growth within your church community?

column4: ## Group Discussion Questions (20-30 Minutes)
column5: ## Group Discussion Questions (20-30 Minutes)

column4: 1.  **Icebreaker Question:** “What is your earliest memory of attending or being part of a church? How has your view of the church changed over time?”
column5: 1.  **Icebreaker Question:** “What is your earliest memory of participating in or belonging to a church? How has your view of the church changed over time?”

column4: 2. **Exploring the Church as the Body of Christ:** Read 1 Corinthians 12:12-27. What does this passage teach us about the church’s unity and diversity? How can we celebrate and honor each other’s differences?
column5: 2. **Exploring the Church as the Body of Christ:** Read 1 Corinthians 12:12-27. What does this passage teach us about the unity and diversity of the church? How do we acknowledge and honor one another’s differences?

column4: 3.  **The Church’s Mission:** How does the church fulfill its upward (worship), inward (edification), and outward (evangelism) purposes? Which area do you feel most called to participate in?
column5: 3.  **The Church’s Mission:** How does the church carry out its upward aims (worship), inward aims (building up/edification), and outward aims (proclaiming the Gospel/evangelism)? In which area do you sense you are particularly called to participate?

column4: 4. **Addressing Conflict and Growth:** Hebrews 12:12-17 calls us to strengthen one another and avoid bitterness. How can we handle division or hurt within the church in ways that foster healing and unity?
column5: 4. **Dealing with Conflict and Growth:** Hebrews 12:12-17 calls us to strengthen ourselves and avoid bitterness. How can we handle division or hurt within the church so that it promotes healing and unity?

column4: 5.  **Finding Your Place:** Think about a time when you felt most connected to your church. What factors contributed to that experience, and how can we create similar experiences for others?
column5: 5.  **Finding Your Place:** Think about a time when you felt deeply connected to your church. What factors led to that experience, and how can we create similar experiences for others?
